narrative:
The model estimates you have a 34% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your background. First, having had no past class failures actually worked in your favor and pulled the prediction toward passing. Second, your strong desire to pursue higher education also pushed the outcome toward passing. However, your father’s secondary-level education was the factor that most strongly pulled the prediction toward failing. Compared with students who passed, this level of parental education is somewhat less common and appears to reflect a home environment with fewer academic resources or expectations, which the model associates with greater risk of underperformance.

Although your family is larger than most, your parents live apart, and you study less than two hours per week—far below the 2–5 hours that most successful students report—these details played smaller roles. The dominant signal came from the combination of no prior failures and high ambition being outweighed by your father’s educational background.

To improve, focus on turning your ambition into concrete habits. Aim to study at least two hours most days, seek extra academic support now rather than later, and talk with your family about how they can help you stay on track. Small, consistent changes in daily study routines can meaningfully shift your chances before the final exams. (248 words)
